cards.front: **What CRM is** — definition, and the sentence that matters most
cards.back:
**"CRM is a strategy for managing a company's interactions with its customers and sales prospects."**

> ### **"CRM is not just about technology."**
> *"It involves **strategy and redesign of business processes**."*

**The goal is a four-stage life cycle:**
$$\textbf{find} \rightarrow \textbf{attract and win} \rightarrow \textbf{retain} \rightarrow \textbf{learn from}$$

| Stage | Application |
|---|---|
| **find** | Marketing Management |
| **attract and win** | Sales Force Automation |
| **retain** | Call Centre · Field Service |
| **learn from** | CRM Analytics |

**The last stage is the one people forget** — feedback *"to better design the company's product and customer facing processes."* **That is what makes CRM a strategy rather than a sales tool.**

cards.front: **"One holistic view of the customer"** — why it matters
cards.back:
Without it, the same customer exists as **several different customers**:

| Department | Knows |
|---|---|
| **Sales** | the deals, the pipeline, discount history |
| **Support** | the complaints, open tickets |
| **Marketing** | which campaigns they responded to |
| **Finance** | what they owe and how late they pay |

**The failure mode:** a salesperson calls to upsell a customer who has an **unresolved complaint and an overdue invoice** — because they cannot see either.

$$\textbf{fragmented customer data} \Rightarrow \textbf{the company contradicts itself in front of the customer}$$

**This is Unit 1's information-silo problem moved to the customer** — Nestlé's 29 vanilla records is the same defect. **ERP unified the internal view; CRM unifies the customer view** — and adds *"from outside the organization if needed, like social media"*, which ERP never claimed.

**Note "in real time"** — a nightly-batch view is useless when the customer is on the phone now.

cards.front: **The sales funnel** — the six stages and what each means
cards.back:
$$\textbf{Leads} \rightarrow \textbf{Prospects} \rightarrow \textbf{Opportunities} \rightarrow \textbf{Customer} \rightarrow \textbf{Account} \rightarrow \textbf{Repeat Sales}$$

| Stage | Means |
|---|---|
| **Lead** | a **name** — someone who might buy. Unqualified |
| **Prospect** | a lead that has been **qualified** — need, budget, authority |
| **Opportunity** *(deal)* | a **specific potential sale**, with value and close date |
| **Customer** | closed — a **Sales Order** exists |
| **Account** *(and Cases)* | an **ongoing relationship**; support tickets are *cases* |
| **Repeat Sales** | revenue without re-acquisition |

**Why a funnel: volume shrinks at every stage** — which makes **conversion rate** the measurable thing, and that is what *pipeline* and *sales forecasting* compute.

> **The Customer → Account transition is where CRM stops being about selling** — the goal changes from *win* to *retain*, and that is the boundary between the sales and service applications.

cards.front: **The ten CRM application areas** — sorted by funnel stage
cards.back:
| Stage | Applications |
|---|---|
| **Find** | **Marketing Management** |
| **Win** | **Sales Force Automation · Product Configuration · Revenue and Pricing · Order Management** |
| **Serve and keep** | **Call Centre · Field Service** |
| **Sell through others** | **Partner Relationship Management** |
| **Sell without people** | **e-Commerce** |
| **Understand all of it** | **CRM Analytics** |

**Two are structurally different from the rest:** **PRM** is CRM applied to **channel partners rather than end customers**, and **e-Commerce** is the channel where **the customer sells to themselves**. Everything else supports a human employee doing something.

cards.front: **Sales Force Automation** — the six capabilities, and why salespeople actually use it
cards.back:
**Contact management · Lead / Opportunity management · Sales forecasting and pipeline · Sales performance management · Territory management · Quote generation** *(plus: Web 2.0 is gaining popularity among SFA vendors)*

| Capability | The problem |
|---|---|
| **Contact management** | *"need not remember contact information of **thousands**"* |
| **Lead / Opportunity mgmt** | which deal deserves my time today? |
| **Forecasting and pipeline** | what will I actually close this quarter? |
| **Territory management** | which accounts are mine? |
| **Performance management** | what did I achieve — **and what am I paid?** |
| **Quote generation** | a correct priced proposal without a week of chasing |

> **The adoption lesson, stated obliquely:** *"tracking sales performance, based on which they are provided **incentive / compensation**."* **An SFA that only helps management see the pipeline gets filled in badly; one that computes commission gets filled in accurately.**

⚠️ **Territory management is really about conflict** — without it, two salespeople call the same prospect and argue over the commission.

cards.front: **Call centre applications** — the eight capabilities and the four questions they answer
cards.back:
**Predefined escalation route · previous records of the caller · support in different time zones and languages · managing call assignments · knowledge base · self service capabilities · workflow · field service management**

| Question | Capabilities |
|---|---|
| **Who should take this call?** | **ACD**, call assignments, **escalation route** |
| **Who is calling, what happened before?** | **previous records** — delivered by **CTI** |
| **How does the agent solve it?** | **knowledge base**, workflow |
| **Does it need to go further?** | **field service management** |

**Technologies:** **LAN · ACD (Automatic Call Distributors) · CTI (Computer Technology Integration) · web integration · IVR (Interactive Voice Response) · voice logging · IVR/speech portals**

> **Without "previous records of the caller", every call starts from zero.** It is **the single customer view arriving in the two seconds before the agent says hello.**

$$\textbf{one agent solves it} \rightarrow \textbf{knowledge base} \rightarrow \textbf{every agent} \rightarrow \textbf{self-service: the customer}$$

cards.front: **Marketing management** — the loop and the six capabilities
cards.back:
$$\textbf{gather and analyse} \rightarrow \textbf{plan and budget} \rightarrow \textbf{execute communications} \rightarrow \textbf{measure results} \rightarrow \textit{(back to gather)}$$

**Capabilities:** **campaign management · customer interaction management · marketing planning · marketing resource and asset management · opportunity / lead management · loyalty marketing**

> **The stage that distinguishes marketing *automation* from marketing is the last one — measurement.** *Half of advertising is wasted and nobody knows which half* is a **measurement** problem, and running campaigns through a system makes response recordable against the customer record.

**The handoff:** *"generate qualified leads for the sales team"* — **marketing's output is SFA's input**, which is why *opportunity/lead management* appears in **both** lists. **That seam failing = unqualified leads dumped on a sales team.**

⚠️ **"Marketing resource and asset management" is not about customers** — it manages the marketing department's **own** budgets, agencies and creative assets.

cards.front: **Field service** — the four constraints that make it hard
cards.back:
The deck states the assignment problem precisely: **which worker → which site → which equipment/problem**, based on **availability and skill**.

| Constraint | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Skill** | not every engineer can service every machine |
| **Availability** | already booked, or driving |
| **Location** | travel time is real and expensive |
| **Parts** | the right spare must be **on the van** |

> **Any three can be satisfied while the fourth fails — and the visit still achieves nothing.**

**Capabilities:** field service management · **scheduling workforce** · **managing spares / service parts** · **mobile solutions capability**

**"Reverse logistics" is the distinctive direction** — the faulty part comes **back** to be repaired, refurbished or scrapped. **Service supply chains move goods both ways.**

**Mobile is a capability, not a preference:** a field engineer is **never at a desk**, so without it data is entered late from memory.

cards.front: **PRM** — why channel selling needs its own application
cards.back:
| | **Direct selling (CRM)** | **Channel selling (PRM)** |
|---|---|---|
| Who meets the customer | **your** salesperson | **the partner's** |
| Who controls them | you — employees | **nobody** — independent business |
| Who sees the end customer | you | **the partner** |

> **You cannot instruct a partner — you can only make it attractive for them to sell your product rather than a competitor's.**

**Every capability is a lever:** partner addition · **distributing leads** · partner profiling · partner programs · opportunity tracking · **special partner discounts** · partner service · **managing channel inventory / partner pipeline**

⚠️ **Channel inventory is the hardest and most valuable:**
$$\textbf{sold to the channel} \neq \textbf{sold to the customer}$$
**That gap is where the bullwhip effect is born** — and mistaking channel stocking for real demand is how you keep producing into a market that stopped buying.

cards.front: **The three types of CRM analytics**
cards.back:
| Analytics | Sits over | Technique |
|---|---|---|
| **Sales analytics** | SFA, orders, pricing | **dashboards displaying KPIs** — descriptive |
| **Marketing analytics** | campaigns, loyalty, leads | **predictive analytics** — segmentation, targeting, **campaign ROI** |
| **Customer service analytics** | call centre, field service | **preventive** — *"correct problems before they affect customer satisfaction"* |

> **Only marketing is described as predictive**, and that is not accidental: **marketing must commit budget in advance of knowing the outcome**, so a prediction has direct value.

**Reporting capabilities:** **dashboards · built-in reports · custom reports · trend analysis · historical comparison · graphics · drilldown**

**Drilldown matters most** — *"sales down 8%"* is useless without *which region, which product, which salesperson.* **It is exactly the OLAP roll-up/drill-down operation: CRM analytics is OLAP with a customer dimension.**

cards.front: **The CRM vendor market** — and why it looks nothing like the ERP market
cards.back:
**Leading products:** **Salesforce · SAP · Oracle · Adobe · Microsoft · Zoho**

**2018 quadrant (Value Score × Capability Score):**
- **Leaders:** **Pipedrive · HubSpot · Salesforce · Zoho**
- **Pacesetters** *(high capability, lower value)*: **Oracle CRM On Demand**, Gold-Vision, amoCRM, Bpm'online
- **Masters:** Highrise, Base, Hatchbuck · **Contenders:** many small players

| | **ERP market** | **CRM market** |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 1 | **SAP, Oracle** | **Salesforce** — a CRM-only company |
| Structure | three tiers, consolidated | **dozens of viable players** |
| Newcomers | rare | **HubSpot, Pipedrive, Zoho are Leaders** |

> **CRM sits at the *edge* of the enterprise, so it needs far less core integration — and low integration requirement is exactly when best-of-breed beats the integrated suite.**

cards.front: **PLM** — what it is, and the parallel that makes it memorable
cards.back:
**"PLM manages all data and information about a product from its initial conception to retirement."**

**The life cycle:** conceptualization → design → manufacturing → **quality throughout** → **safety during manufacture, distribution and usage** → service → **retirement from service**

**Cross-functional because it involves: R&D, Engineering, Marketing, Production, Quality, Sales and Service.**

| Module | Life cycle of | From | To |
|---|---|---|---|
| **HCM** | **an employee** | recruitment | retirement |
| **CRM** | **a customer** | lead | repeat customer |
| **PLM** | **a product** | **conception** | **retirement** |

> **All three are the same architectural idea: one long-lived entity, one record, every function that touches it.**

$$\textbf{one product} \times \textbf{seven functions} \Rightarrow \textbf{seven partial views, unless something unifies them}$$

cards.front: **PLM business drivers** — the four groups
cards.back:
| Group | Drivers | The pressure |
|---|---|---|
| **More products, less time, less money** | product variants & growing product lines · **shorter development cycles** · cost reduction pressure · **reduced engineering resources** | **do more with less, faster** |
| **More people involved** | collaboration with local and global partners · process and data integration between R&D, Production, Supply | **designed across organisations** |
| **More rules to obey** | **regulatory compliance pressure** | safety and environmental law |
| **More to protect and record** | **intellectual asset management** · **documentation control** · innovation focus | **the design *is* the asset** |

**The first group is a squeeze from both ends** — more variants, more products, less time, fewer engineers. **Those four cannot all be satisfied by working harder; the only way is to stop re-designing what exists.**

**PLM's three current capability areas** *(from Unit 3's evolution table)*: **Product Data Management · Document Management · Product Safety.**

**Market:** **SAP PLM · PTC Windchill.**

cards.front: **SCM** — definition, and the phrase that separates it from ERP
cards.back:
**"SCM is the oversight of materials, information, and finances as they move in a process from supplier to manufacturer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer."**

> **"Coordinating and integrating these flows both *within and among* companies."**

**ERP optimises inside one company. SCM optimises across companies that do not share a management, a system or an incentive** — a fundamentally harder problem, because you cannot instruct your supplier.

$$\textbf{MRP: one factory} \rightarrow \textbf{MRP II: one company} \rightarrow \textbf{ERP: one enterprise} \rightarrow \textbf{SCM: the network}$$

**Goal:** *"reduce cost of inventory and efficient movement of materials."*

**Also known as IRP — Intelligent Resource Planning** *(deck-specific label; SCM is the term everyone uses).*

**Includes:** inventory management · warehouse management · transportation management. **Current-day SCMs support "open data models"** — suppliers see your inventory, customers see order status. **That is the precondition for VMI and CPFR.**

cards.front: **The three flows** and **the seven rights**
cards.back:
| Flow | Direction | Contents |
|---|---|---|
| **Material movement** | **downstream** | goods from supplier to customer |
| **Information / documentation** | **both ways** | mandatory forms, import/export, licence-permit; **orders up, delivery status down** |
| **Financial tracking** | **upstream** | payment schedules, COD handling |

$$\textbf{goods flow down} \qquad \textbf{money flows up} \qquad \textbf{information flows both ways}$$

> **Information is the flow that can be improved almost for free — and better information substitutes directly for inventory.** Every technique in this chapter trades one for the other.

**The seven rights:** the right **product · quantity · condition · place · time · customer · price**

**They are seven ways one delivery can be wrong** — getting six of seven right still means it failed.

**Terms:** **WIP · ASN · GRN · AWB / Bill of Lading · VMI · 3PL**

cards.front: **SCOR** — the five processes and the two features of the diagram
cards.back:
**SCOR = Supply Chain Operational Reference**

$$\textbf{Plan} \cdot \textbf{Source} \cdot \textbf{Make} \cdot \textbf{Deliver} \cdot \textbf{Return}$$

The diagram draws them repeating along: **Suppliers' Supplier → Supplier → Your Company → Customer → Customer's Customer**, with **Plan** above, spanning the chain.

**① The same five repeat at every link.** **Your *Deliver* is your customer's *Source*** — which is what makes it a **reference model**: one vocabulary so two trading partners can describe their processes in the same terms. *(The goods-issue/goods-receipt symmetry from Unit 4, generalised.)*

**② Plan sits above and spans further.** **Source, Make, Deliver and Return are executed locally; Plan is what has to be shared** — which is exactly the SCP-vs-SCE split.

**③ Return is a first-class process**, because reverse logistics is real and expensive.

*(The deck's aside: "Have we seen this slide earlier? — **BPM!**" — SCOR is a Unit 2 process-modelling standard.)*

cards.front: **The three planning levels** — horizon, question, tools
cards.back:
| Level | Cadence | **The question** | **Tools** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Strategic** | **yearly / quarterly** | *long term capacity strategy? most optimized **network design**?* | **Network Design · LTP** |
| **Tactical** | **monthly / weekly** | *how do I meet monthly customer requirements?* | **S&OP · MPS · MRP** |
| **Operational** | **daily / hourly** | *how do I schedule my orders, my transport routes?* | **detailed scheduling · transportation planning · route scheduling** |

**Strategic:** factory geography, warehouse locations, procurement sources — **"difficult to reverse without substantial cost"**, influencing long-term profit and sales goals.
**Tactical:** months to quarters. **Operational:** reviewed week/daily — vendor schedules, distribution and transport plans.

> **The separator is reversibility, not just time.** A factory is bricks; a route is a line on a map. **Time horizon and reversibility go together because the longer the horizon, the more concrete the commitment.**

⚠️ **The whole MRP II ladder sits inside ONE of SCM's three levels.**

cards.front: **Why strategic decisions have maximum impact** — and the reversed axis
cards.back:
**"Strategic supply chain decisions have maximum impact on business."** The chart plots **ROI / Impact** against **Planning Horizon**, running **Years → Quarters → Month → Days → Hours**.

$$\textbf{network design} \Rightarrow \textbf{which lanes exist} \Rightarrow \textbf{what routes can be optimised}$$

> **No amount of brilliant route optimisation recovers the cost of a warehouse in the wrong city.** The operational planner chooses the best path through a network **someone else already fixed** — so the ceiling on operational savings is set strategically.

⚠️ **The deck flags that the *time axis direction is reverse to usual*** — years on the left, hours on the right, so impact **falls** rightward. **Reading it without noticing inverts the conclusion.**

**And it notes the *overlaps* in the three plans** — the boundaries are gradients, exactly as Unit 3 said of MRP II's five levels.

**High-reliance industries: Retail · distributed manufacturing.**

cards.front: **The SCP evolution ladder** — MRP II → ERP → SCM
cards.back:
| Generation | Capabilities |
|---|---|
| **MRP II** | material requirement calculation · machine/labour resource · **SOP · MPS · ATP · DRP** · capacity planning |
| **ERP** | all of MRP II **+ Demand Planning + integration with SCM execution systems** |
| **SCM Planning & Collaboration** | **Advanced** Demand Planning · **Supply Chain Planning and Optimization** · production scheduling optimization · **Transportation Planning, Route Optimization** · **Global ATP** · **Advanced Collaboration (VMI, CPFR)** |

**Each rung adds one word:**
- **MRP II** → **calculation**
- **ERP** → **integration**
- **SCM** → **optimization and collaboration**

| MRP II / ERP | SCM |
|---|---|
| Demand Planning | **Advanced** Demand Planning |
| Order Promising (ATP) | **Global** ATP |
| Distribution Plan (DRP) | Transportation Planning, **Route Optimization** |

> **Every SCM entry is an ERP entry with "advanced", "global" or "optimization" attached** — the *transaction → decision* movement again. ***"DRP has quickly grown to become an application by itself"* — a feature became a product category.**

*("Term SCM became popular post 1995.")*

cards.front: **SCP vs SCE** — the test, and the asymmetric Applications row
cards.back:
| | **Planning** | **Execution** |
|---|---|---|
| Produces | **a plan** — numbers about the future | **a transaction** — a record that something happened |
| Can be re-run | **yes, freely** | **no** — a posted GR is a fact |
| Needs | optimisation algorithms | **authorisation, workflow, audit trail** |
| **Applications** | **ERP *or* SCP solutions** | **ERP only** |
| Vendors | SAP APO, i2, Oracle APS, ERPs | SAP ERP, Oracle ERP |

> **Does anything physically happen?** That is the test.

**The deck's reason for the asymmetry:** *"planning software need not worry about **access control, transaction management, workflow execution** — these are the must/should features of execution software such as ERP."*

> **Specialist planners exist; specialist executors do not.**

⚠️ **The boundary is soft** — *"transportation planning and shipping"*. **The discriminator: planning decides *what should happen*; execution records *what did*.**

cards.front: **ERP vs SCP** — the nine-row table, and what it really is
cards.back:
| | **ERP** | **Supply Chain Planning** |
|---|---|---|
| **Focus** | transaction and basic planning | **advanced planning and optimization** |
| **Planning order** | **sequential** material then capacity | **simultaneous** |
| **Prioritization** | **cannot handle** any rule | **any rule** (customer, product) |
| **Simulation** | limited | **extensive** |
| **Constraints** | **cannot do** constraint-based planning | **can** |
| **Capacity** | **infinite capacity** | **finite capacity** |
| **Forecasting** | basic | **statistical / causal models** |
| **Replanning** | **takes long** | **very quick** |
| **ATP** | limited | **alternate location / alternate product** |

> **Every row is one of MRP's seven limitations from Unit 3, answered.**

**Sequential vs simultaneous is the key one:** MRP plans material first then checks capacity — **which is why closed-loop MRP loops back to MPS. SCP plans both in one pass, so the loop disappears.**

**The deck's verdict:** *"**SCP has advanced functionality over ERP; but ERP has higher integration and execution capability.**"*

cards.front: **The eight SCP modules** — and the three levels they map to
cards.back:
| Level | Modules |
|---|---|
| **Strategic** | **Network design** |
| **Tactical** | **Demand planning · Supply Network planning · Production planning** |
| **Operational** | **Detailed scheduling · Transportation planning · Vehicle Scheduling · Route Planning** |

**One strategic, three tactical, four operational** — the granularity gets finer and the module count rises as the horizon shortens, exactly as in MRP II's five levels.

**Network design decisions:**
- **where new locations (plants, warehouses, DCs, stores) shall be opened**
- **which products at which locations**
- **which customers to which distribution centers**
- **capacity requirements**
- **which locations shall be closed**

**Two kinds:** *where things are* (open, close, capacity) and *how the network is used* (product-to-plant, customer-to-DC). **The second is the cheapest lever — it can be changed without building anything.**

**Triggers:** expanding to another country · demand shifts making locations unprofitable · **a new product**. *"SCP is not a one-time static exercise."*

cards.front: **The network design service-vs-cost trade-off** — the four numbers
cards.back:
| | **Optimal Network For Cost** | **Optimal Network For Service** |
|---|---|---|
| **Savings** | **\$6 million** | **\$3 million** |
| **Service** | **40% next day** | **80% next day** |

$$\textbf{Doubling next-day service } (40\% \rightarrow 80\%) \textbf{ costs } \$3\text{m of the }\$6\text{m saving}$$

> **There is no "right" answer between them.** The cost-optimal network **consolidates into few large facilities**; the service-optimal one **spreads into many local ones.**

**Same trade-off as DRP's competing objectives, Level vs Chase, and service-level-based inventory. Four appearances of one structure.**

**What the optimiser provides is the *curve*, not the answer** — the cheapest network for each service level. **Choosing a point is a business decision**, which is why the deck notes *"cost optimization is key **but weighed against risks** — a variety of what-if situations have to be allowed."*

**Optimum location costs:** transportation · production · storage · handling · procurement · **penalty costs for delayed/non-fulfilled demand** · fixed operating · opening/closure · **government subsidies**

cards.front: **Demand planning** — three techniques ERP lacks
cards.back:
**① Causal / multi-variate models**
$$\textbf{time-series: } y_t = f(y_{t-1}, y_{t-2}, \dots) \qquad \textbf{causal: } y_t = f(\text{price}, \text{weather}, \text{promotion}, \dots)$$
**The difference bites whenever the future is not like the past — which is when a forecast matters most.**

**② Like modelling** — forecast a product **with no history** by borrowing a similar one's. **A new phone model has no history; the previous model does.** This is what makes *planning for new products* possible.

**③ Consensus vs collaborative forecasting**

| | Reconciles | Across |
|---|---|---|
| **Consensus** | sales, marketing, finance, production | **inside one company** |
| **Collaborative** | your forecast and your **customer's** | **across companies** |

**Consensus is S&OP made into software; collaborative becomes CPFR.**

⚠️ **"Planning for Discontinuation / Phase out" is the forgotten one** — extrapolating a dying product's history **over-orders right to the end**, creating exactly the obsolete stock the KPI measures.

**And SCM stores forecast history in a data warehouse; ERP does not** — which is why the DW-BI chapter is in the same unit.

cards.front: **Production scheduling** — setup/sequence optimization and the three approaches
cards.back:
**On many machines, changeover time depends on what ran before.** Paint white→black is quick; **black→white needs a deep clean.**

$$\textbf{same jobs, different sequence} \Rightarrow \textbf{different total setup time} \Rightarrow \textbf{different capacity available}$$

> **MRP cannot see this at all** — it schedules by due date and treats setup as fixed. **A scheduler that sequences light-to-dark creates capacity out of nothing but ordering.**

**Which is why the benefits are three at once — *reduced lead times, reduced stocks, improved on-time delivery*.** Normally those trade against each other; **better sequencing removes waste rather than reallocating it.**

| Approach | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Heuristics** | sensible rules — earliest due date, shortest job. **Fast, no guarantee** |
| **Optimization algorithms** | search for the best sequence. **Better, more computation** |
| **Bottleneck scheduling** | **schedule the constraint first**, fit everything else around it |

**Bottleneck scheduling rests on one observation: an hour lost at the bottleneck is an hour lost by the whole factory; an hour lost elsewhere costs nothing.**

cards.front: **Global ATP** — the escalating search, and ATP vs CTP
cards.back:
**ERP's ATP:** *"an online search to verify the company's ability to provide the requested product, in the requested quantity, on the date requested"* — **"limited, based on static info."**

**GATP's six capabilities are an escalating sequence of answers to *"can I have it by Friday?"*:**

| If… | GATP tries |
|---|---|
| not in **this** warehouse | **alternate location** |
| **this product** unavailable | **alternate products** |
| **nothing finished** exists | **capable-to-promise** — can we *make* it? |
| the answer depends on **who is asking** | **rule based availability check** |
| the date depends on shifts | **calendars** |

$$\textbf{ATP: is there stock or a planned receipt?} \qquad \textbf{CTP: could we produce it, given components and capacity?}$$

**CTP requires exactly what SCP has and ERP lacks — finite capacity and multi-level component visibility.**

**"Rule based" is commercially interesting:** when stock is short, **who gets it?** **First-come-first-served is a policy, not a law of nature.**

cards.front: **Transport planning** — three optimisation areas and the constraint list
cards.back:
| **Technology** | **Business Need** | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| **Transport planning and vehicle scheduling** | **minimize number of vehicles used** | when and what size vehicle to order, given the shipment plan, service level and capacity |
| **Route optimization** | **minimize vehicle travel distance** | optimum route with **multiple drop points**, shortest path hitting all |
| **Optimum truck load building** | **minimize unloading labour; truck does not run empty** | takes account of **drop sequence** and **material properties** — *light must not sit below heavy* |

**Constraints:** vehicle capacity · depot location · limits of distance/duration/stopovers · handling resources · max storage time · **vehicle types (trains, ships, aircraft, trucks)** · **opening hours of locations** · **drop sequence** · **stacking constraint** · **access restriction**

> **Load building and routing are coupled through drop sequence — the last delivery is loaded first, deepest in the truck. You cannot decide the packing until you know the route.**

⚠️ ***"Route optimization is one of the most complex problems in computer science"*** — it is the **vehicle routing problem**. And **access restriction** *(border crossings allowed only at certain hours)* shows **the optimiser is scheduling in time, not just routing in space.**

cards.front: **The three kinds of collaborative planning**
cards.back:
| Kind | Shares | When |
|---|---|---|
| **Collaborative forecasting** | **what we expect to need** | **before** anything is ordered |
| **Collaborative replenishment** | **what we are actually consuming** | **as** it happens |
| **Collaborative product development** | **what we are designing** | **before the product exists** |

**The tyre example makes the forecasting case unanswerable:** a tyre manufacturer's demand is **completely determined by its customers' vehicle production plans** — **dependent demand across a company boundary.** Forecasting it statistically is guessing at something already known, **by someone else**.

> **Collaboration converts an independent-demand problem into a dependent-demand one. It moves Unit 3's line outward.**

**Why collaborate at all:** *"a supplier of a business may be a customer of another business"* — the SCOR recursion. **Optimising your own link is optimising a fragment.**

$$\textbf{local optimum at every link} \neq \textbf{optimum for the chain}$$

⚠️ **And it is often asymmetric:** *"customer businesses **force** the supplier to adopt automated collaboration channels."*

cards.front: **VMI** — the definition and the process
cards.back:
**"VMI is a process where the supplier makes inventory replenishment decisions for the customer."** The vendor **monitors the buyer's inventory levels** and decides **which items, how much, when**.

> ### **"In VMI, the customer does not generate a P.O."**

| | **Normal procurement** | **VMI** |
|---|---|---|
| Who decides | **customer** | **supplier** |
| Who raises the order | customer → **PO** | supplier → **CRP order** |
| What the customer sends | **a purchase order** | **stock, sales and promotion data** |

**The EDI flow:** customer sends **stock data · past sales data · planned promotions** → supplier builds a **sales forecast**, decides replenishment, determines quantity *(considering transport load qty)* → **CRP order sent via EDI** → customer **reviews and may change** → acknowledgement → supplier processes and sends **ASN** → customer prepares for receipt. **Payment by electronic fund transfer.**

**History: popularized in the late 1980s by Wal-Mart and Procter & Gamble.**

> **The supplier now sees *actual consumption* rather than *a filtered order signal*** distorted by the retailer's batching and safety stock. **That is why eliminating the bullwhip is the first benefit.**

cards.front: **VMI benefits and difficulties**
cards.back:
**Benefits:**
1. **Eliminating bullwhip effect — less variability**
2. **Uniform production for supplier**
3. **Lower administration cost**
4. **Lower transportation costs**
5. **Lower inventories**
6. **Increased sales and service**
7. **Suppliers know real market demand information**

> **Six of the seven follow from the seventh:**
$$\textbf{suppliers know real demand} \Rightarrow \textbf{less variability} \Rightarrow \textbf{uniform production} \Rightarrow \textbf{lower inventories and transport costs}$$
*(Lower admin cost comes from a different cause — **no PO, no invoice matching, no order chasing**.)*

**Difficulties:**
- **Unstable pricing environment / sudden surge in demand are difficult to handle** — VMI extrapolates consumption, and **the customer is no longer ordering, so there is no signal that the world changed.** *(Hence *planned promotions* is one of the three EDI feeds.)*
- **VMI requires a critical volume of business (% of supply)** — **the saving is proportional to volume while setup cost is fixed.**

**That threshold is why VMI is a Wal-Mart-and-P&G story rather than a universal practice.**

cards.front: **CPFR** — the nine steps and the pattern that makes them memorable
cards.back:
> ### **Agree, then forecast twice, then order.**

| Phase | Steps |
|---|---|
| **Plan** | ① **Develop Collaboration Arrangement** ② **Create Joint Business Plan** |
| **Forecast (sales)** | ③ Create ④ **Identify Exceptions** ⑤ **Resolve Exceptions** |
| **Forecast (order)** | ⑥ Create ⑦ **Identify Exceptions** ⑧ **Resolve Exceptions** |
| **Replenish** | ⑨ **Generate Order** |

**Steps 3–5 and 6–8 are the SAME three steps applied to two different forecasts.**

$$\textbf{Sales forecast} = \text{what the consumer will buy}$$
$$\textbf{Order forecast} = \text{what the retailer will order}$$
**They are not the same number** — 1,000/week sold may be 4,000 ordered monthly. **The sales forecast is smooth; the order forecast is lumpy — and that gap is where the bullwhip is born.**

⚠️ **Four of nine steps are exception handling.** **Without them CPFR would just be two forecasts exchanged by email — the exception process is what makes it a *single* forecast.**

**VICS = Voluntary Intra Industry Commerce Standards** — the 9-step reference framework.

cards.front: **The bullwhip effect** — why it amplifies upstream
cards.back:
$$\textbf{Consumer Sales} \rightarrow \textbf{Retailer's Order} \rightarrow \textbf{Wholesaler's Order} \rightarrow \textbf{Manufacturer's Order}$$
**with progressively larger swings at each step.**

| Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Order batching** | sell 100/day, order **500 weekly** — smooth demand becomes spiky order |
| **Safety stock adjustment** | demand +10% → order +10% **plus more safety stock** |
| **Lead-time reaction** | long lead times → over-order to cover uncertainty |
| **Promotions / forward buying** | a large one-off order not reflecting consumption |
| **Shortage gaming** | expecting rationing, buyers **over-order deliberately** |

> **Every cause has the same root: each link sees only the orders from the link below, not actual consumption.**

**Which is exactly why VMI eliminates it** — the supplier receives **POS data and stock levels, not orders. The distorting filter is removed.** And **CPFR** attacks it with a **shared forecast**, so the manufacturer is not inferring demand from an order pattern at all.

**Both techniques replace an order signal with a data signal.**

cards.front: **SCM vendors** — and what the list quietly documents
cards.back:
**i2 / JDA** *(strong in **Retail**)* · **SAP APO** · **Oracle APS / Value Chain Planning** · **Manugistics / JDA** · **Adexa** · **Demantra** · **Logility** · **Aspentech** *(strong in **Process Industry**)* · **IFS** · **IBM's ILOG SCO**

**SAP APO's six modules map one-to-one onto this chapter:** **Demand Planning · Supply Network Planning · Global ATP · PP/DS · Transportation Planning · Deployment**, under the **Supply Chain Cockpit**.

**i2's suite is far longer** because it is separately-sold products — note **Global VMI** and **3D Load Configurator** as products in their own right.

⚠️ **Both "i2 / JDA" and "Manugistics / JDA" appear on one list** — two once-independent vendors, both now JDA. The deck's note: *"being 'smaller' compared to ERP systems, there is **more churn by way of mergers/acquisitions**."*

> **The financial-viability criterion demonstrated inside a single slide** — and why *"ERP vendors claim advantage of integration to ERP."* **IBM's ILOG SCO is positioned to "complement and enhance existing investments in ERP and APS"** — best-of-breed stated explicitly.

cards.front: **The data warehouse** — definition and the four characteristics
cards.back:
> **"A data warehouse is a subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant, non-volatile collection of data used in support of the management decision making process."**

**Mnemonic: SITN — and each is a deliberate rejection of how an operational system works:**

| Characteristic | Meaning | OLTP does the opposite |
|---|---|---|
| **Subject-oriented** | organised around **sales, product, customer** | organised by **process** |
| **Integrated** | built from **OLTP, ERP, CRM, legacy** | one application |
| **Time-variant** | **historical perspective, past 5–10 years** | current state only |
| **Non-volatile** | **data once recorded cannot be updated until the next refresh** | updated constantly |

> **Non-volatile is the least intuitive and most important:** if a warehouse overwrote, **last year's report would silently change every time someone corrected a record today — and no analysis would be reproducible.**

**It holds four levels of detail simultaneously:** **current detail · old detail · lightly summarized · highly summarized.**

cards.front: **The three-tier DW architecture** — and how it delivers the four characteristics
cards.back:
$$\textbf{Data Sources} \rightarrow \textbf{ETL / Data Migration} \rightarrow \textbf{Data Storage Repository} \rightarrow \textbf{Reporting, OLAP, Data Mining}$$

The deck's diagram: **CRM · Billing · ERP · Flat Files · Other Sources → ETL → Data Warehouse → Reporting · Analytics · Data Mining**, with **Data Marts** and **OLAP Servers (MOLAP, ROLAP)** between warehouse and tools.

| Characteristic | Delivered by |
|---|---|
| **Integrated** | **the ETL layer** |
| **Subject-oriented** | **the warehouse schema** — star schemas |
| **Time-variant** | the warehouse accumulating loads |
| **Non-volatile** | **the load process** — periodic batch |

**Separating the tiers buys three things:** analytical load **never touches production systems** *(hence "better performance of source system" as a stated advantage)* · sources can change without breaking reports · **one warehouse serves many tools**.

**Pros:** common data model · clean data · better source performance · facilitates reporting
**Cons:** **data latency** · **unstructured data reporting not possible**

cards.front: **Why both DW disadvantages follow from its advantages**
cards.back:
**① Data latency is the price of non-volatility.**
$$\textbf{non-volatile + batch load} \Rightarrow \textbf{latency}$$
The warehouse is **always out of date by one refresh cycle** — ask it about this morning's orders and it will not know. ***Which is why an ODS exists*** — *"a near real time integrated view of current data."*

**② Unstructured data is excluded by the schema.** A warehouse stores facts and dimensions in tables; **emails, documents, images, call recordings and social media posts do not fit** — and they are exactly the data CRM said could be valuable.

> **Saying that both disadvantages are consequences of the design, not oversights, is the mark-earning observation.**

**And "better performance of source system" is the advantage people forget** — it benefits the *operational* systems, not the analysts. **Moving reporting off OLTP is often the original business case, before anyone runs a single analysis.**

cards.front: **Star schema** — facts, dimensions, attributes and the worked example
cards.back:
**Fact** — **numeric measurements representing a business aspect**, stored in the **fact table at the centre**. **Dimension** — **qualifying characteristics giving additional perspectives**, joined by **foreign key**, **many-to-one**. **Attribute** — **additional information for a dimension** *(customer name, city, region for the Customer dimension)*.

**The deck's worked schema:**

| Table | Columns |
|---|---|
| **SALES** *(fact)* | Product_Code · Period_Code · Store_Code · **Units_Sold · Dollars_Sold · Dollars_Cost** |
| **PRODUCT** | Product_Code · Description · Color · Size |
| **PERIOD** | Period_Code · **Year · Quarter · Month · Day** |
| **STORE** | Store_Code · Store_Name · City · Telephone · Manager |

$$\textbf{fact table} = \textbf{keys pointing outward} + \textbf{numbers to add up}$$

**The test:** **facts are things you *add up*; dimensions are things you *group by* or *filter on*.**

**PERIOD's attributes ARE the drill-down path** — attributes are the axes along which you roll up and down. **And keeping text out of the fact table keeps it narrow, which is what makes a billion-row table fast.**

cards.front: **Why the star schema is deliberately denormalised**
cards.back:
| | **OLTP — normalized** | **Warehouse — star schema** |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | **avoid update anomalies** | **avoid joins** |
| Because | data changes constantly | **data is non-volatile — it does not change** |
| Cost | many joins per query | some storage redundancy |

> **The justification is non-volatility.** Normalisation exists to prevent inconsistency **when data is updated — and warehouse data is not updated.** So the reason for normalising evaporates, and you may trade storage for query speed freely.

Exactly what the OLTP/OLAP table states: *"OLTP database design is **highly normalized**… OLAP is **denormalized with limited tables**."*

**Advantages of the star schema:** **optimized for reporting** · **lets the user view facts from a variety of perspectives (dimensions)**

cards.front: **Granularity, refresh and quality data**
cards.back:
**Granularity trade-off:**
$$\textbf{summarized: fast, cheap, cannot drill down} \longleftrightarrow \textbf{detailed: slow, expensive, answers anything}$$
**Summarized** — reduced storage and CPU, better reporting performance, **but cannot answer transaction-level questions.** **Detailed** — every transaction available, **but too voluminous.**

> **The unrecoverable direction is what matters: you can always summarise detail; you can never recover detail from a summary.**

**Refresh options:** **periodically** *(nightly, weekly)* · **after every significant event** *(e.g. month-end closing — business meaning, not clock time)* · **on every update** *(near real time)*
**Techniques:** **full refresh** *(simple, impractical at scale)* · **incremental / delta refresh** *(cheap, needs change capture)*

**Properties of Quality Data:** **Accuracy · Completeness · Integrate · Timeliness · Consistency and Standardization · Accuracy of Hierarchical relationships · Uniqueness**

⚠️ **Uniqueness = Nestlé's 29 vanilla records as a property. Hierarchical accuracy matters because a mis-assigned city makes every regional report wrong — invisibly at the summary level.**

cards.front: **ETL** — what each step does, and where the warehouse's promises are kept
cards.back:
| Step | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Extract** | **batch extraction of high volumes from one or more sources** |
| **Transform** | **modify per specific business logic** so it can go to the target |
| **Load** | **load to target systems** — DW, data mart, ODS, another application |

> **Transform is where the four characteristics are actually manufactured:**

| Transform does | Delivering |
|---|---|
| reconciling customer IDs | **Integrated · Uniqueness** |
| standardising formats, units, currencies | **Consistency and Standardization** |
| restructuring process data into subjects | **Subject-oriented** |
| stamping records with a load date | **Time-variant** |

**Extract and Load are plumbing; Transform is the work.**

**Four usage areas:** **data migrations** *(the ERP project's master and transaction objects!)* · **master data management** · **data warehousing and reporting** · **compliance**

**Vendors — three backgrounds:** pure-play (**Ascential DataStage, Informatica PowerCenter**) · database vendors (**IBM, Microsoft, Oracle OWB**) · BI vendors (**Business Objects, Cognos, Hummingbird, SAS**)

cards.front: **OLTP vs OLAP** — the seven-row table and the one difference it all follows from
cards.back:
| **OLTP** | **OLAP** |
|---|---|
| **current data** | **historical data** |
| **detailed data** | **detailed AND highly summarized** |
| **dynamic — changes every transaction** | **largely static** |
| **transaction driven** | **analysis driven** |
| **day-to-day decisions** | **strategic decisions** |
| **large number of operational users** | **low number of managerial users** |
| **high number of transactions** | **medium to low** |

$$\textbf{OLTP: many users, tiny operations, constant writes} \qquad \textbf{OLAP: few users, huge queries, rare writes}$$

| Because the workload is… | The design must be… |
|---|---|
| **many small writes** | **normalized** — cheap writes, no anomalies |
| **few enormous reads** | **denormalized** — no joins, fast reads |

**The two user rows are the most telling** — *thousands of clerks* vs *a few dozen managers*. **Tuning one database for both means it serves neither.**

⚠️ ***"OLAP database is formed from various databases which are OLTP in nature"*** — **OLAP has no data of its own.**

cards.front: **OLAP operations** — the five functionalities with the deck's own examples
cards.back:
| Operation | What it does | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Roll up** | **aggregate to a higher level** | City → State → Region |
| **Drill down** | **expose detail** | Region → State → City |
| **Slice** | **fix ONE dimension** | *"the **Food** slice"* |
| **Dice** | **fix ranges on SEVERAL dimensions** | Food+Personal care, APAC+Europe, Retail |
| **Pivot** | **rotate the axes** | Products-as-rows → Regions-as-rows |

$$\textbf{Slice cuts one flat plane out of the cube; dice cuts a smaller cube out of the cube.}$$

**The deck's location hierarchy:** **Country (India) → Region (West) → State (Maharashtra) → City (Mumbai) → Sales office**
**The CPG cube:** Product *(detergent, food, personal care, healthcare)* × Sales Channel *(retail, wholesale, export)* × Regions *(APAC, Americas, Europe)*

**Types of analysis:** **aggregation · comparison · ranking**
**Strengths:** powerful visualization · **fast interactive response** · **good for time series** · finds clusters and outliers

cards.front: **ROLAP · MOLAP · HOLAP**
cards.back:
| Type | Storage | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **ROLAP** — **Relational** OLAP | data stays in **relational tables**; cubes computed on the fly | **scales to huge volumes**; **slower** queries |
| **MOLAP** — **Multidimensional** OLAP | data pre-aggregated into a **multidimensional cube** | **very fast**; **limited size**, long loads |
| **HOLAP** — **Hybrid** OLAP | **summaries in a cube, detail left relational** | fast at summary, **drills through to detail** |

> **The middle letter gives it away** — **R**elational, **M**ultidimensional, **H**ybrid.

**HOLAP is the granularity trade-off implemented as an architecture** — the summarised side's speed *and* the detailed side's answerability.

**MOLAP and ROLAP are named in the architecture diagram as the two OLAP *server* types**, sitting **between the warehouse and the user**. **The warehouse stores; the OLAP server presents.**

cards.front: **Data mart** — what it is and how it relates to the warehouse
cards.back:
**"A subset of a data warehouse that supports the requirements of a particular department or business function."**

**Characteristics: small · flexible · lightly summarized · departmentally structured**

**Differences from a warehouse:** focuses on **one department**; **does not normally contain detailed operational data**; **more easily navigated** because it holds less.

**Advantages** reduce to two: **relevance** *(the data they need, in their form)* and **size** *(faster response, easier cleansing and loading, cheaper to implement)*.

$$\textbf{many sources} \rightarrow \textbf{one warehouse} \rightarrow \textbf{many data marts}$$

> **The warehouse fans data in; the marts fan it back out — so the integration happens ONCE, centrally.** The marketing mart and the finance mart are guaranteed to agree because both descend from the same reconciled warehouse.

⚠️ **Building marts directly from source systems is the failure mode this prevents** — independent marts drift apart, and you re-create the information silo inside the analytics layer.

cards.front: **ODS** — the warehouse with two characteristics deliberately reversed
cards.back:
**"An ODS consolidates data from multiple source systems and provides a near real-time integrated view of current data."** Its purpose is **operational**, and it has **add, change or delete functionality.**

| Characteristic | **Data Warehouse** | **ODS** |
|---|---|---|
| **Integrated** | ✔ | ✔ **same** |
| **Subject-oriented** | ✔ star schemas | ✘ **flat, transparent tables; no facts or dimensions** |
| **Time-variant** | ✔ 5–10 years | ✘ **only very recent information** |
| **Non-volatile** | ✔ never overwritten | ✘ **overwrite function** |

$$\textbf{Warehouse: "what has been happening over years?"} \qquad \textbf{ODS: "what is true right now, across all systems?"}$$

> **The ODS is the answer to data latency** — the warehouse's stated disadvantage.

**"Overwrite function" is listed as an *advantage*** — **the same property is a virtue or a defect depending on the question.** And *"save data at a document level"* pairs with *"relatively simple queries on small amounts of data"*: **the ODS answers *what happened to this one thing*, not *what is the trend*.**

cards.front: **Data mining** — the four properties of a pattern, uses and steps
cards.back:
**"Data mining is the process of extracting patterns from data."**
> **"Data Warehousing provides the enterprise with memory; Data Mining provides the enterprise with intelligence."**

**Patterns must be: valid · novel · potentially useful · ultimately understandable**

| Property | Rules out |
|---|---|
| **Valid** | **statistical noise** |
| **Novel** | what you **already knew** |
| **Potentially useful** | what you **cannot act on** |
| **Understandable** | what **nobody can interpret** |

> **Novelty distinguishes mining from reporting: reporting answers questions you asked; mining finds patterns you did not know to ask about.**

**Uses:** customer analysis · targeted marketing · **cross selling** · segmenting customers · **market basket analysis** · credit rating · **fraud detection** · medicine/disease outcome

**Steps: Data Preparation → Model Construction → Results validation**

⚠️ **"Results validation" is not optional** — search a large dataset and you *will* find patterns by chance. **A pattern must be tested on data it was not discovered in.**

**Vendors:** Clementine · IBM Intelligent Miner · SGI MineSet · SAS Enterprise Miner

cards.front: **Analytics vs BI** — what each adds
cards.back:
**Analytics** = *"business applications that analyze data for **specific business subjects**"* — SCM, CRM, HR, Finance.

$$\textbf{OLAP: a general tool} \qquad \textbf{Analytics: a packaged application for one function}$$

**Segments:** ① **Financial and BPM** *(Financial Analytics + Business Performance Management)* ② **CRM Analytics** ③ **Operations and Production**

**Two categories:** **descriptive** *(focuses on history)* and **prescriptive** *(focuses on trends to predict)*. ⚠️ *(The deck says "prescriptive" where industry usually says **predictive**.)*

---

**BI is the umbrella:** *"OLAP, Analytics, Data mining etc. are part of the Business Intelligence suite."*

**What BI adds is *pushing* rather than *pulling*:** **alerts · scorecards · dashboards · workflow · data delivery** *(plus ad hoc query, report customization by user profile, predictive modeling, visualization, slice and dice)*.

> **OLAP waits for someone to ask. Alerts and dashboards bring the answer without them asking** — which is what *"correct problems **before** they affect customer satisfaction"* requires.

**Vendors — another acquisition story: Business Objects → SAP · Cognos → IBM · Hyperion → Oracle.**

cards.front: **Common vs industry-specific processes** — the dividing line
cards.back:
$$\textbf{common} = \textbf{how a company runs itself} \qquad \textbf{specific} = \textbf{what the company actually does}$$

**Common across industries:** financial accounting · management accounting · corporate governance · **HR — recruitment, payroll, talent management** · corporate services like travel management · quality management · **global trade — import procedure, documentation, customs** · warehouse and transport management

**The deck's own contrast:** an **oil and gas company** needs **exploration**, meaningless to a consumer goods company. **Product promotion** matters to consumer goods but **"may not make any sense for a petroleum company where prices in countries like India are mostly dictated by government."**

> **Every company pays people, keeps accounts, complies with law and moves goods** — which is exactly Unit 3's *"across the whole enterprise"* group. **The core operating process is where industries diverge.**

**That is the commercial basis of the industry-solution market** — and why *"industry specific functionality"* can override an entire package-selection process.

cards.front: **Oil & gas** — the value chain and the two uniquely exclusive processes
cards.back:
$$\textbf{Upstream} \rightarrow \textbf{Mid-Stream} \rightarrow \textbf{Refining} \rightarrow \textbf{Primary Distribution} \rightarrow \textbf{Secondary Distribution} \rightarrow \textbf{Service Station Retailing}$$
with product streams **Crude · Refined Products & LPG · Lubes · Natural Gas**

**Processes:** exploration · developing petroleum fields · refinery operations · lubes manufacturing · **oil and gas commodity trading** · bulk transport of inflammable materials · terminals management · service station operations / fuel management · **convenience retailing**

**ERPs: Aspentech · SAP IS-Oil**

⚠️ **Two genuinely industry-exclusive entries from the SAP solution map:**
- **Joint Venture Management** — oil fields are **too expensive and risky for one company**, so consortia share costs and revenues by share. **No generic ERP has this.**
- **Exchange & Throughput Handling** — oil companies **swap product with competitors** rather than transport it. *You give me a tanker in Chennai; I give you one in Mumbai.*

**"Optimize Product Mix"** has no discrete-manufacturing equivalent — **one barrel yields a whole slate of products simultaneously.**

cards.front: **Automotive, pharma, consumer goods and mining** — the distinctive processes
cards.back:
**Automotive:** **Kanban planning for multiple models on one line · Warranty Management · Just in sequence deliveries · Vehicle information and life cycle · Dealer Business · Car Leasing**
> **JIS: parts arrive *in the order the line will use them*, not merely on time.** Requires the supplier to see your line schedule in near real time — **deeper than VMI or CPFR.**

**Pharma:** **Patent Management · IP · Clinical trial management · LIMS · Secure Tracing / E-Pedigree · Regulatory compliance submission · Secrecy of Formulation**
> Every one exists because of **regulation** or **intellectual property**. **E-pedigree defeats counterfeits** — batch traceability at pharmaceutical stakes. **"Secrecy of formulation" constrains the ERP's own access design.**

**Consumer goods:** distribution planning · **trade promotions** · brand management · **many SKUs** · contract manufacturing · **collaboration with retailers** · route management · **DSD** · food safety · **cold chain** · **empties and returns** · **markdowns** · fashion/style/design
> **Nine of thirteen are distribution or retail** — the mineral-water question answered.

**Mining:** safety · **explosives** · remote logistics · transport optimization · **washing/beneficiation** · **blending** · commodity pricing and auctions · **CSR** · exploration
> **ERPs: SAP IS-Mine · Mincom · Gemcom.** **Beneficiation has variable yield — no discrete BOM can express it.**

cards.front: **Retail** — processes, and what the Retek list reveals
cards.back:
**Processes:** **category management · merchandise budgeting and planning · assortment management · space management · advanced promotion planning and markdowns · store clustering · continuous replenishment, cross docking · point of sale solutions · cross channel order fulfilment · store operations**

**ERPs: Retek · JDA · SAP IS-Retail**

**Store clustering makes the rest tractable** — 800 individual assortment plans is impossible; one national plan ignores real differences. **A few dozen cluster decisions instead.**

⚠️ **The Oracle Retek product list is this entire course, re-badged:**

| Retek product | What it is |
|---|---|
| **RETL** | **ETL** |
| **Retail Data Warehouse** | **the data warehouse** |
| **RDF** — Retail Demand Forecasting | **demand planning** |
| **AIP** — Advanced Inventory Planning | **inventory models** |
| **ReIM** — Retail Invoice Matching | **three-way matching** |
| **RIB** — Retail Integration Bus | **EAI** |
| **VCC** — Value Chain Collaboration | **CPFR / VMI** |

> **An industry solution is not different technology — it is the same technology with the industry's vocabulary, data model and processes pre-configured.**

cards.front: **Healthcare, education, banking, insurance & utilities**
cards.back:
**Healthcare — providers:** medical records · **appointment scheduling · bed planning · operation theatre** · inpatient/outpatient tracking · waiting lists · patient help desk · online diagnostic reporting
**Healthcare — payers:** **claims handling · payer relationship management · payer communication**
> ⚠️ **"Manage Resources" includes *organs, blood*** — inventory items that are **perishable in hours, non-substitutable and impossible to reorder.** The extreme critical-item case. **And *"Payer Relationship Management" is CRM where the customer is an insurer.***

**Education modules:** **Admission → Registration → Grading → Progression → Degree → Graduation → Alumni Relations**, with **Financial Aid** throughout.
> **The fourth life-cycle module in this course** — after H2R, lead-to-customer and concept-to-retirement. **"Alumni Relations" is the Customer → Account transition.**

**Banking:** savings/cards/deposits · shares, bonds, derivatives · brokerage · **loans, project financing, LOC, leasing** · **treasury: interest rate, FX, credit risk**
> **ERPs: Finacle (Infosys) · FLEXCUBE (Oracle) · IS-Banking (SAP) · BaNCS (TCS).** **In a bank the financial transaction IS the product — the ledger is the operation.**

**Insurance:** CRM · policy management · **claims management** · commissions · **Inkasso/Exkasso** · investment management
**Utilities:** **managing meters, reading and consumption determination · energy trading · billing · waste and emission** *(Ramco for Utilities)*

cards.front: **Cloud computing** — advantages, the criticism, and the layers
cards.back:
**"Computing infrastructure is available on demand… a way of computing, via internet."** Customers **do not own the physical infrastructure**, avoiding capex by **renting usage and paying only for what they use.**

**Advantages:** cost reduction · **improvement in efficiency and utilization** · **centralization of infrastructure** · **companies need not design hardware based on peak load** · scalability · easier maintenance · better reliability · measuring resource usage · **available anytime anywhere**

$$\textbf{on-premise capacity} = \textbf{peak demand} \qquad \textbf{cloud capacity} = \textbf{current demand}$$

**Providers pool many customers whose peaks fall at different times — so the same hardware serves everyone's peak.** *(The capacity-planning problem from Unit 3, solved for computing.)*

⚠️ **The criticism is a genuine argument:** *"companies might **save on upfront capital but might actually pay more for operating expenses** — so where the capital expense is relatively small, the cloud model may not make great financial sense."* **Cloud converts CapEx into OpEx, and rent never stops.**

**Areas:** Database · Desktop · Disaster recovery · **Infrastructure** · Integration · **Platform** · Storage as a service. **IaaS → PaaS → SaaS: each layer rents more and controls less.**

cards.front: **SaaS** — the characteristic that generates all the others
cards.back:
**"A provider licenses an application to customers for use as a service on demand, through time subscription or *pay-as-you-use*."**

**Characteristics:** network-based access · **maintenance managed centrally, not at each customer site** · **one-to-many delivery model** · **priced per user**, with a minimum and extra fees for bandwidth/storage

$$\textbf{one instance of the software} \longrightarrow \textbf{many customers}$$

| Because one-to-many… | …this follows |
|---|---|
| maintenance happens once | **central management** |
| everyone on the same version | **faster releases for the whole community** |
| hardware shared | **multi-tenant efficiency — never idle** |
| **cannot change shared code** | **customization is impossible** |

**Benefits:** entirely variable cost, **no upfront investment — easy to calculate ROI** · multi-tenant efficiency · faster feature releases · flexibility and scalability

**Drivers:** SMB adoption of packages · **computing has become a commodity** · **popular for applications more standard across industries** · matured software evolution · matured hosting · **reliable network, bandwidth and security**

**Started with SFA and CRM**, then billing, invoicing, HR, service desk, sales pipeline.

cards.front: **SaaS vs Hosted ERP** — the seven-row table and why ERP resisted SaaS
cards.back:
| Criteria | **SaaS** | **Hosted ERP** |
|---|---|---|
| **Architecture** | **Multi Tenant** | **Single Tenant** |
| **Fee** | **Subscription** | **License** |
| **Licence ownership** | **ERP Vendor** | **Customer** |
| **Customization possible** | **No** | **Yes** |
| **Hosted by** | **ERP vendor's data center** | **Service provider's data center** |
| **Upgrades by** | **ERP vendor** | **Customer** |
| **Maintenance by** | **ERP vendor** | **Service provider** |

> **All seven follow from row one.**

**Hosted ERP suits:** *"customers looking to outsource their existing implementation to avoid capital outlays, and customers **lacking access to knowledgeable ERP staff**."* **You have already customised and own the licence — keep your system, rent someone else's operations team.**

**2013 reality (Panorama):** **On-Premise 61% · SaaS 14% · Cloud ERP 12% · Other 13%.**

**Why ERP resisted:** **security of customer data** · **high availability — ERP is the heart of operations** · **each customer needs customization, hard to stick to a standard solution**

> **The resolution: "industry best-practice configurations, plus the ability for the customer to do further configuration." Configuration, not code.**

cards.front: **Enterprise services & SOA** — the seven principles in three ideas
cards.back:
**A service is a business function:** *"each of these services is **actually a business function**"* — *check credit*, *create sales order* — which is why it is *"understood both by business executives and IT staff."* **Web Services are the building block**, accessible over standard internet protocols, **independent of platform and language**.

**SOA principles:**

| Idea | Principles |
|---|---|
| **Break it into pieces** | **modularity · componentization** |
| **Make the pieces fit** | **composability · interoperability · standards-compliance** |
| **Keep the pieces independent** | **loose coupling · re-usability** |

**Loose coupling is load-bearing** — a service can be replaced without breaking its callers, because they depend on its **interface**, not its internals.

**Benefits:** respond faster to market conditions · **reuse** · **simplified testing** *(services fully tested by the publisher)* · integration savings · platform-independent access

⚠️ **The strategic one:** *"SOA opens up opportunities for **thousands of small niche vendors**… now they can build applications quickly integrated with SAP or Oracle."* **By making integration cheap, SOA lowers the barrier to entry for specialists** — part of why best-of-breed stayed viable.

cards.front: **RFID** — components, advantages over bar code, and disadvantages
cards.back:
**Components:** **Tags** *(**active** — includes a power source; **passive** — no power, relies on readers)* · **Reader** *(emits a radio signal via an antenna)* · **Antenna** *(transmits signals and captures scan readings)*

**Advantages over bar code:**
1. **No line of sight required** — bar codes need each item presented in a particular orientation, close to the scanner
2. **Hundreds of characters vs 12–15 digits**
3. **Rewritable thousands of times** — data can be **added at each supply-chain node**; a printed bar code is **frozen**
4. **Reduced manual labour** — reads items **kept deep inside boxes**

$$\textbf{bar code: an identifier} \qquad \textbf{RFID tag: a travelling record}$$

**Disadvantages:** **bar codes are mature; RFID needs to stabilize on standards** · **the main barrier is the cost of the tag**

**Supply chain benefits:** tracking of items · **reduced shrinkage** · better replenishment · **efficient reverse logistics** · **improved inventory, receiving and shipping accuracy**

> **Every benefit is a Unit 4 KPI improved** — and **improved accuracy has knock-on value**, because the whole inventory pyramid runs on the control layer's numbers.

cards.front: **EAI vs point-to-point** — and the journey to ERP II
cards.back:
**EAI** = *"an integration framework composed of technologies and services that form a **middleware** to enable integration of systems and applications across the enterprise"*, linking applications on **different operating systems, databases and languages**.

$$\textbf{point-to-point: } \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \textbf{ interfaces} \qquad \textbf{hub: } n \textbf{ interfaces}$$

| Systems | **P2P** | **Hub** |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | **10** | **5** |
| 10 | **45** | **10** |
| 20 | **190** | **20** |

**The gap widens quadratically** — and in P2P, **changing one system's format means changing every interface that touches it.**

**Products:** IBM WebSphere Business Integration · Microsoft BizTalk · **SAP NetWeaver PI** · Oracle Fusion Middleware · Sterling Commerce · Tibco

---

**ERP → ERP II:** *"ERP's focus was **enterprise-centric**, internal resource optimization and transactional processing. **ERP II has a new focus on process integration and external collaboration.**"* **"Collaborative commerce with suppliers and customers is the heart of ERP II."**

**Three drivers = the three technologies:** **extending outside** → SOA · **anywhere anytime** → mobile/cloud · **one interface to best-of-breed** → EAI
